title: Deprivation of liberty, restraint and restrictive practice
blurb: Use the least restrictive option, apply the MCA conditions for restraint, and know how DoLS authorisations work.
question: Mrs Gill, 87, has delirium and lacks capacity to understand her risk of falling. At night she keeps trying to climb out of bed. A colleague suggests raising the bed rails. What is the most appropriate response?

teach.h: Restriction needs a legal basis and a good reason
teach.body: Every restriction on a person's freedom engages their human rights, especially Article 5 (liberty) and Article 8 (private life). The MCA lets you act in the best interests of a person who lacks capacity, but restraint is allowed only under extra conditions (s6), and anything that amounts to a deprivation of liberty in a hospital or care home needs authorisation under the Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards (DoLS). In plain English: use the least restriction possible, for the shortest time, for the person's own protection.
teach.cite: MCA 2005 s1(6), s5, s6, Sch A1; HRA 1998 Art 5

rows.label: Force
values: Holding an arm for an injection

rows.label: When resisted
values: To make P do something P resists

teach.caption: Restraint includes restricting movement whether or not the person resists.

steps.label: Best interests
steps.sub: Reasonable belief the act is in P's best interests (s5)

steps.label: Necessary
steps.sub: Reasonably believed necessary to prevent harm to P

steps.label: Proportionate
steps.sub: To the likelihood and seriousness of that harm

teach.caption: Fail either s6 condition and the MCA gives no protection for the act.

levels.label: Find the cause: pain, toileting, delirium
Environment: low bed, crash mat, lighting

teach.caption: MCA s1(6): consider whether the purpose can be achieved as effectively in a less restrictive way.

teach.body: Mrs Gill is restless at 02:00. Bed rails would restrict her movement and could cause a worse fall if she climbs over them. The nurse first checks for causes (pain, a full bladder, delirium triggers), then uses a low bed with a crash mat, a night light and closer observation. This achieves the purpose, reducing injury, in a less restrictive way (s1(6)). The plan, and the reasons, are recorded and reviewed.

items: Use it only if de-escalation and other preventive strategies have failed and harm is likely; keep de-escalating (NICE NG10 1.4.5).
Never use it to punish, inflict pain or establish dominance (1.4.6).
Avoid taking the person to the floor; if prone is unavoidable, keep it as short as possible (1.4.24).
No pressure on the neck, chest or abdomen; protect airway, breathing and circulation (1.4.25).
One person leads, monitors the airway and vital signs; debrief afterwards (1.4.32, 1.4.55).

teach.text: Restraint is not only hands-on. Bed rails, lap belts, locked doors, removing walking aids and sedation given to manage behaviour (chemical restraint) all restrict a person. Each must meet the same tests: best interests, necessary to prevent harm to the person, proportionate, and the least restrictive option.

items: Restraint (s6): force or threat of force against resistance, or restricting movement whether or not resisted.
Lawful only if necessary to prevent harm to P and proportionate to that harm, in P's best interests.
Always try the less restrictive option first (s1(6)); find the cause of distress.
DoLS: hospitals and care homes, 18+; urgent up to 7 days, standard up to 1 year; LPS not in force.
Physical restraint: last resort, no pressure on airway, chest or abdomen, monitor, debrief, record.

summary: You can now recognise the many forms restraint takes, apply the MCA s6 conditions and the least restrictive principle, and describe how DoLS authorisations are requested and how long they last. You also know the safety rules if physical restraint is unavoidable.

A.q: A student asks when it is lawful under the MCA to restrain an adult who lacks capacity, for example by holding his hand to stop him pulling out a cannula. What is the best answer?
options: When a doctor has prescribed it in the medical notes
When the family have given their written consent to it
When it is necessary to prevent harm and proportionate
When it is needed to protect the staff caring for him
A.why: MCA s6: restraint is permitted if the person reasonably believes it is necessary to prevent harm to P and it is a proportionate response to the likelihood and seriousness of that harm, in P's best interests.

whyNot.0: A prescription does not meet the s6 conditions by itself.
whyNot.1: Family consent does not make restraint lawful for an adult.
whyNot.3: s6 refers to preventing harm to the person themselves, not to staff.

A.q: Mrs Gill, 87, has delirium, lacks capacity and keeps trying to climb out of bed at night. Which intervention is most appropriate?
options: Raise both bed rails and check her every hour overnight
Use a low bed with a crash mat and closer observation
Ask the doctor for a sedative to help her sleep through
Tuck the sheets tightly so she cannot easily get out
A.why: MCA s1(6): consider a less restrictive way to achieve the purpose. A low bed, crash mat and closer observation reduce injury risk without confining her.

whyNot.0: Bed rails restrict movement and she may climb over them, risking a worse fall.
whyNot.2: Sedation to manage behaviour is chemical restraint and not the least restrictive first step.
whyNot.3: Tightly tucked sheets restrict her movement and could trap her.

A.q: A ward manager in England is updating training on people who lack capacity and whose care in hospital amounts to a deprivation of liberty. Which scheme currently provides the legal authorisation?
options: The Liberty Protection Safeguards
Section 5 of the Mental Capacity Act
A best interests decision by the consultant
The Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards
A.why: DoLS (MCA Schedule A1) remain the scheme in force in hospitals and care homes in England and Wales. The Liberty Protection Safeguards have not been implemented.

whyNot.0: LPS were legislated in 2019 but have not been brought into force.
whyNot.1: Section 5 protects acts of care and treatment but does not authorise a deprivation of liberty.
whyNot.2: A best interests decision alone does not authorise a deprivation of liberty.

B.q: A care home manager concludes that Mrs Lowe's care arrangements amount to a deprivation of liberty and that an authorisation is needed immediately. What may the managing authority do?
options: Give an urgent authorisation lasting up to 7 days
Give a standard authorisation lasting up to 1 year
Ask her son to sign a consent to the arrangement
Apply for a deputy to be appointed by the court
B.why: MCA Sch A1 paras 76-78: where the need is urgent, the managing authority gives an urgent authorisation (up to 7 days) and requests a standard authorisation from the supervisory body.

whyNot.1: Standard authorisations are given by the supervisory body, not the care home.
whyNot.2: A relative cannot consent to a deprivation of liberty for an adult.
whyNot.3: A deputy does not authorise a deprivation of liberty in a care home; DoLS does.

B.q: Mrs Hart, 83, has dementia and lacks capacity. For three nights she has called out repeatedly. A colleague suggests asking for a sedative "so the bay can get some sleep". What is the most appropriate response?
options: Agree, as other patients also have a right to rest
Agree, if her family are happy for it to be given
Assess for pain, constipation and delirium first
Move her to a side room and close the door at night
B.why: Sedating someone to control behaviour for others' convenience is chemical restraint, which must be in her best interests and the least restrictive option (MCA s1(5)-(6)). Distress often has a treatable cause.

whyNot.0: Others' needs matter, but the intervention must be in Mrs Hart's best interests.
whyNot.1: Family agreement does not make chemical restraint lawful or appropriate.
whyNot.3: Shutting her away is restrictive and does not address the cause.

B.q: On a dementia ward, Mr Payne, 81, lacks capacity and was briefly held by two trained staff to stop him hitting another patient. What should the nurse record?
options: That he was aggressive and needed restraint
His behaviour, with a request for sedation
That staff followed the trust's restraint policy throughout
Why the hold was used, how, how long, his response
B.why: Code 10.1-10.4: accurate, timely records. Restraint must be justified as necessary and proportionate (s6), so the record shows why, how, for how long and its effect, supporting review and debrief (NICE NG10).

whyNot.0: This is a conclusion without the detail needed to justify or review the hold.
whyNot.1: A sedation request is not a record of the restraint.
whyNot.2: A statement of policy compliance does not show what actually happened.

C.q: During a hold, a patient is taken to the floor face down. What is the most important safety action for the staff member leading the hold?
options: Kneel across the back to stop the patient struggling
Turn the patient supine or end prone as soon as possible
Keep the hold in place until the patient stops resisting
Place a hand over the mouth to stop the patient biting
C.why: NICE NG10 1.4.24-1.4.25: avoid the floor; use supine if possible, and if prone is necessary use it for as short a time as possible; never compromise airway, breathing or circulation.

whyNot.0: Pressure on the back or chest can compromise breathing and circulation.
whyNot.2: Restraint should be for the shortest time possible, with continued de-escalation.
whyNot.3: Obstructing the mouth interferes with breathing and communication.

C.q: Daniel, 24, has a learning disability and becomes agitated in a busy emergency department. He is shouting and pacing but has not hurt anyone. What is the most appropriate first response?
options: Call security so that he can be held safely if needed
Give oral medication to calm him before he escalates
Move him somewhere quieter and use calm de-escalation
Ask his support worker to take him outside for a walk
C.why: Restrictive interventions are a last resort; first reduce triggers and use de-escalation, applying the least restrictive option (MCA s1(6); NICE NG10 1.3.14, 1.4.5).

whyNot.0: Preparing to restrain before de-escalation has been tried is not least restrictive.
whyNot.1: Medication is considered after verbal de-escalation, not first.
whyNot.3: His support worker may help, but leaving the department may delay his assessment and does not address the trigger.

C.q: Mr Okoro, 79, lacks capacity and lives in a care home under a standard DoLS authorisation. His nurse wonders who has been appointed to represent him under DoLS. Who is this?
options: His relevant person's representative
His care home's registered manager
The local authority's best interests assessor
His GP as the professional who knows him best
C.why: MCA Sch A1 para 139: the supervisory body must appoint a relevant person's representative after a standard authorisation is given, to maintain contact with and represent the person.

whyNot.1: The manager runs the managing authority and is not independent of the arrangement.
whyNot.2: The best interests assessor carries out an assessment; they are not the ongoing representative.
whyNot.3: A GP is not appointed as representative under DoLS.

reteach.title: Ask: what is the least I can do to keep this person safe?
reteach.question: Before you restrict anyone, which questions must you be able to answer?

blocks.body: 1) Does the person lack capacity for this decision? 2) Is it in their best interests? 3) Is it necessary to prevent harm to THEM, and proportionate to how likely and serious that harm is? 4) Is there a less restrictive way? If the restriction amounts to a deprivation of liberty in a hospital or care home, it also needs a DoLS authorisation.

blocks.text: Sedation to quieten a ward is chemical restraint, not 'treatment'. It needs the same justification.

explain.body: Using or threatening force to make a person do something they resist, or restricting their liberty of movement whether or not they resist (MCA s6(4)). Includes bed rails, belts, locked doors and chemical restraint.

test.q: A resident who does not resist has a lap belt fastened in her chair. Is this restraint under the MCA?
options: No, because she is not resisting
No, if her family requested it
Yes, if it is used for over an hour
Yes, as it restricts her movement
test.why: s6(4)(b): restricting a person's liberty of movement is restraint whether or not they resist.

whyNot.0: Resistance is not needed for restriction of movement to be restraint.
whyNot.1: A family request does not change what restraint is.
whyNot.2: The Act sets no time threshold for restraint.

explain.body: Restraint is protected by the MCA only if the person reasonably believes it is necessary to prevent harm to P, and it is a proportionate response to the likelihood and seriousness of that harm.

test.q: Which factor determines whether restraint is proportionate under s6?
options: How busy the ward is at the time
The likelihood and seriousness of harm
Whether the family have been informed
The grade of the staff carrying it out
test.why: s6(3): the act must be a proportionate response to the likelihood of P suffering harm and the seriousness of that harm.

whyNot.0: Staffing pressures do not make restraint proportionate.
whyNot.2: Informing the family is good practice but not the s6 test.
whyNot.3: Staff grade is not part of the legal test.

explain.body: For people aged 18+ lacking capacity in hospitals and care homes. The managing authority requests a standard authorisation from the supervisory body (local authority in England) and can give itself an urgent authorisation of up to 7 days. Standard authorisations last up to 1 year.

test.q: In England, which body gives a standard DoLS authorisation for a hospital patient?
options: The hospital trust as managing authority
The Care Quality Commission
The local authority as supervisory body
The Court of Protection
test.why: MCA Sch A1 para 180: for hospitals in England the supervisory body is the local authority (usually where the person is ordinarily resident); it gives standard authorisations.

whyNot.0: The managing authority requests the authorisation and can give an urgent one only.
whyNot.1: The CQC monitors DoLS but does not grant authorisations.
whyNot.3: The court can authorise deprivation of liberty in other settings, but hospital and care home standard authorisations come from the supervisory body.

explain.body: Last resort only after de-escalation fails; never to punish; avoid the floor and prone position; no pressure on neck, chest or abdomen; a lead monitors airway and vital signs; debrief afterwards (NICE NG10).

test.q: Which action is part of safe practice immediately after a restrictive intervention?
options: Writing a brief note at the end of the shift
Holding a post-incident debrief once safe
Withholding the person's leave as a consequence
Asking the person to apologise to staff involved
test.why: NICE NG10 1.4.55: once risks are contained, hold an immediate post-incident debrief to identify harm, ongoing risk and the emotional impact on everyone involved.

whyNot.0: Records should be made as soon as possible, not left to the end of the shift (Code 10.1).
whyNot.2: Restrictive interventions must not be used as punishment (NG10 1.4.6).
whyNot.3: Demanding an apology is punitive and not part of safe practice.
